title: 1.1 INTRODUCTION TO MATRICES

blocks.text: The word ‘matrices’ is plural of the word ‘matrix’. The term matrix was first introduced by the mathematician Arthur Cayley in 1860. The knowledge of matrices is necessary in the various areas of Mathematics. It has widely been used in the fields of pure mathematics, statistics, engineering and physical and social sciences. Thus, matrix theory finds an important place in modern age and has become an integral part of mathematics.
Matrices make presentation of numbers clearer and make calculations easier. The following table presents the information about a series of hockey matches played between Pakistan and India.

The information is readily available when presented in this way. For example, if we want to know how many matches India lost against Pakistan, we go along the row ‘India’ and column ‘Lost’ and find that it is 4. Similarly, if we want to know how many matches Pakistan drew with India, we go along the row ‘Pakistan’ and column ‘Drawn’ and find that it is 1. As long as we remember what each number represents, we could remove the row and column headings and write just the numbers, enclosing them in square brackets or parenthesis such as
Let us denote this by A.

blocks.text: 1.1.1 Matrix
A matrix is a rectangular array (arrangements) of real numbers enclosed in square brackets. Each number in a matrix is called an element or entry of the matrix. For example

title: 1.1.3 Order (or dimension) of a Matrix

blocks.text: 1.1.3 Order (or dimension) of a Matrix
A matrix with m rows and n columns has order m × n (read “m by n”).
If a matrix has order m × n then m represents the number of rows and n represents the number of columns.
For example, consider
The order of the matrix A is 2-by-3 or A is a 2-by-3 matrix. Similarly the order of the matrix B is 2-by-2 or B is a 2-by-2 matrix.
Do You Know?
Row 1: 6, 10. Row 2: 5, 3. Row 3: 5, 2. Column 1: 6, 5, 5. Column 2: 10, 3, 2. An element of the matrix: 3 (row 2, column 2).
Dimension of this matrix is 3 × 2.
Remember: Sometimes we will prefer to write the order of a matrix as m-by-n or sometimes (m × n).
Note: Order of a matrix m × n does not mean to multiply m & n.
Tid-Bit: Order of a matrix is also called dimension or size.

steps:

1.1.4 Equality of two Matrices
Two given matrices A and B are said to be equal if:
(i) Both the matrices are of the same order i.e. they respectively have the same number of rows and columns.
(ii) The elements in the corresponding positions in A and B are equal.

title: Exercise 1.1

problems.question:
Which of the following are square and which are rectangular matrices?
(i) A = [[2, 3], [0, 5]]
(ii) B = [[6, 3, -1], [1, 5, 2]]
(iii) C = [[1, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, 0, 1]]
(iv) B = [-5]
(v) E = [-3, 4]
(vi) E = [[-1], [7]]
problems.solution:
SpaceBook supplementary solution (not printed on this exercise page):
A matrix is square if the number of rows equals the number of columns (m = n).
A matrix is rectangular if the number of rows does not equal the number of columns (m ≠ n).

(i) A has 2 rows and 2 columns (2×2): m = n => Square Matrix.
(ii) B has 2 rows and 3 columns (2×3): m ≠ n => Rectangular Matrix.
(iii) C has 3 rows and 3 columns (3×3): m = n => Square Matrix.
(iv) B = [-5] has 1 row and 1 column (1×1): m = n => Square Matrix.
(v) E = [-3, 4] has 1 row and 2 columns (1×2): m ≠ n => Rectangular Matrix.
(vi) E = [[-1], [7]] has 2 rows and 1 column (2×1): m ≠ n => Rectangular Matrix.
problems.answer: (i) Square, (ii) Rectangular, (iii) Square, (iv) Square, (v) Rectangular, (vi) Rectangular.

problems.question:
List the order of the following matrices:
(i) A = [[1, 2, -1], [3, 4, 2]]
(ii) B = [-4]
(iii) C = [[2, 3, -1], [1, 2, 5]]
(iv) F = [[2, 1], [3, 2], [4, -1]]
(v) E = [3, 2]
(vi) D = [[1, 2, 3], [6, 5, 9], [0, 0, 0]]
problems.solution:
SpaceBook supplementary solution (not printed on this exercise page):
The order of a matrix having m rows and n columns is m × n:
(i) A has 2 rows and 3 columns => Order: 2 × 3 (or 2-by-3).
(ii) B has 1 row and 1 column => Order: 1 × 1 (or 1-by-1).
(iii) C has 2 rows and 3 columns => Order: 2 × 3 (or 2-by-3).
(iv) F has 3 rows and 2 columns => Order: 3 × 2 (or 3-by-2).
(v) E has 1 row and 2 columns => Order: 1 × 2 (or 1-by-2).
(vi) D has 3 rows and 3 columns => Order: 3 × 3 (or 3-by-3).

problems.question:
Which of the following matrices are equal.
A = [[2, 5], [1, 3]]
B = [[2, 5], [4, 3]]
C = [[1+1, 3+2], [4, 2+1]]
D = [[2, 4+1], [1, 3]]
problems.solution:
SpaceBook supplementary solution (not printed on this exercise page):
Simplify matrices C and D:
C = [[1+1, 3+2], [4, 2+1]] = [[2, 5], [4, 3]].
D = [[2, 4+1], [1, 3]] = [[2, 5], [1, 3]].

Compare:
- Matrix A = [[2, 5], [1, 3]] has identical entries to D = [[2, 5], [1, 3]] => A = D.
- Matrix B = [[2, 5], [4, 3]] has identical entries to C = [[2, 5], [4, 3]] => B = C.

[[2, -3], [u, 0]] = [[v, -3], [5, w]]

- Position (1, 2): -3 = -3
- Position (2, 1): u = 5 => u = 5

problems.question: If [[x+3, z+4, 2y-7], [-6, a-1, 0], [b-3, -21, 0]] = [[0, 6, 3y-2], [-6, -3, 2c+2], [2b+4, -21, 0]], find the values of a, b, c, x, y, and z.
problems.solution:
SpaceBook supplementary solution (not printed on this exercise page):
Equating corresponding elements:
1) x + 3 = 0  =>  x = -3
2) z + 4 = 6  =>  z = 2
3) 2y - 7 = 3y - 2  =>  -y = 5  =>  y = -5
4) a - 1 = -3  =>  a = -2
5) 0 = 2c + 2  =>  2c = -2  =>  c = -1
6) b - 3 = 2b + 4  =>  -b = 7  =>  b = -7

problems.question:
Solve the following equation for a, b, c, d.
[[a+b, b+2c], [2c+d, 2a-d]] = [[-1, 4], [8, 0]]
problems.solution:
SpaceBook supplementary solution (not printed on this exercise page):
Equating corresponding elements:
(1) a + b = -1
(2) b + 2c = 4
(3) 2c + d = 8
(4) 2a - d = 0  =>  d = 2a

From (4) and (3): 2c + 2a = 8 => a + c = 4 => c = 4 - a
From (1): b = -1 - a
Substitute b and c into (2):
(-1 - a) + 2(4 - a) = 4
-1 - a + 8 - 2a = 4
7 - 3a = 4 => -3a = -3 => a = 1.

Now substitute a = 1:
b = -1 - (1) = -2
c = 4 - 1 = 3
d = 2(1) = 2.

blocks.text: e) Zero matrix or Null matrix
Any matrix (weather it is rectangular or square) of which all the elements (entries) are equal to zero is said to be a Zero matrix or a Null matrix. Thus

blocks.suffix: are some examples of zero matrices or null matrices.

blocks.text: The following points are very important to remember.
i) A zero or null matrix is not necessarily a square matrix.
ii) A null matrix is generally donated by O.
iii) Sometimes we prefer to put the order of a null matrix as a proper subscript with the general symbol O.

The role of the Zero matrix in matrix manipulation is very similar to that of Zero in ordinary algebra. Provided that they are compatible for multiplication (compatibility of multiplication in matrices will be discussed later on in this chapter), the product of any matrix and the Zero matrix is a zero matrix. When working with matrices involving zero matrices, we choose a zero matrix of such an order which is suitable for solving the problem in hand.

title: Diagonal matrix / Scalar matrix

blocks.text: f) Diagonal matrix
A square matrix in which all elements are zero except the diagonal elements is known as diagonal matrix. For example

g) Scalar matrix
A square matrix in which all the elements lying on the main diagonal of the matrix are equal and the remaining elements off the main diagonal are all zero is called scalar matrix.
Equivalently scalar matrix can also be defined as under:
A diagonal matrix in which all the diagonal elements are equal is said to be a scalar matrix.

h) Identity matrix

The identity matrix (sometimes called the unit matrix) is a square matrix and is denoted by I. It is characterized by the fact that all elements on its main diagonal are 1’s whereas all other elements are zero. Sometime it is useful to write the order of the identity matrix as a subscript of I. thus

blocks.suffix: is the identity matrix of order 2.
is the identity matrix of order 3.

blocks.text: When there is no danger of ambiguity the identity matrices I₂ & I₃ are simply denoted by I.
